content_metadata.description: The video features Richard Pearson, a decorated Navy SEAL veteran, recounting his life journey, experiences in the Vietnam War, and personal reflections on missed opportunities. Through a series of personal anecdotes, he offers insights into the challenges and camaraderie of military life, while highlighting the importance of responsibility and education.

qAndA.answer: He wore black pajamas, similar to the clothing worn by the enemy, making it difficult to distinguish between sides.
qAndA.question: What was unusual about the uniform Richard Pearson wore in Vietnam?

qAndA.answer: Bob Henry was hit by a booby trap intended for Richard Pearson, who had asked him to switch places due to his own leg injury.
qAndA.question: Why did Richard Pearson's friend, Bob Henry, get injured?

qAndA.answer: The booby trap blew off the boy's leg. Richard Pearson rushed him to the hospital, where a skilled doctor saved his life.
qAndA.question: What happened to the young boy who tripped the booby trap?

qAndA.answer: He was given a large quantity of toys, clothes, and crutches, which he then donated to SEAL Team to help those in need in Vietnam.
qAndA.question: What surprising gift did Richard Pearson receive at the football game?

qAndA.answer: He regrets not taking full advantage of the educational opportunities available to him while serving. He encourages viewers to learn from his mistake and prioritize their education.
qAndA.question: What does Richard Pearson regret about his time in the military?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: My name is Richard Andrew Pearson.
Lieutenant Commander in the United States Navy retired.
SEAL Team 1.
My childhood wasn't the normal you see on television.
It was very, very sad.
When I turned 17, I went to Houston, Texas and joined the Navy.
The first uniform I wore when UDT.
And throughout SEAL Team was a bathing suit.
But in combat, I wore the same clothes
that the enemy wore in Vietnam, which was just black pajamas.
I had no education, but I knew how to work.
And I always took the worst job available.
I knew there was only one way to go.
And that was up SEAL Special Forces Marine Recon,
Air Force Special Unit.
They all worked together, and I was just good.
Because in my time, they wouldn't work together.
We had a boat that we called the Mighty Mole.
I was the Mortarman.
But my legs were bad, so I had my friend Bob
and he changed places with me.
He took a round in the Mortar pit and was paralyzed.
It should have been me.
Children of all nations are good.
This little boy tripped a booby trap showing us
where his fiat con had run in Blue's Lego.
I rushed him back to the hospital, Dr. Gatelock,
the real hero.
He put him back together, but he didn't have
out of official legs, but we got crutches for him.
He had a smile on his face.
I took his picture with me.
Tough.
My coach, Pop won a football.
My wife said they want you to come to the football game.
Well, they surprised me with tons of toys, clothes,
crutches.
And we ended up taking all that to seal team
and we built a wooden four by eight box.
And we put it on our airplane when we went back
and took it up there.
I think the only thing that I would do differently,
I would have paid more attention to the opportunities
that the military provides for getting a formal education.
The teachers that you have are just that.
They're teachers.
They're not authoritarian.
They're getting all their information from books or papers
or social media.
You have to take it upon yourself to read
the history of our country.

Vision of Vets is honored to present our interview with Dick Pearson, U.S. Navy SEAL.
